title: What was a fraction called in ancient India?
description: An old page from ancient India writes one half as one number above another, with no line. The old name for a fraction tells us what a fraction is. Keeko's doubt is that the line was always there.
teaching_notes: One idea: the old Indian name for a fraction, and the old Indian way of writing it. Watch for the slip that the line between the top number and the bottom number was always there.

source: Do you know what a fraction was called in ancient India?
video_script.why: The child connects a fraction as a roti broken into equal pieces to the old Indian names for a fraction, and learns where our way of writing fractions came from.
video_script.substitution: A roti broken into equal pieces, the book's own object: each piece is a part of the whole, which is what the old names describe.
video_script.anchor: an old manuscript page from ancient India with a fraction written one number above another
video_script.wrong_answer: the line between the numbers was always there
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the line between the numbers was always there. The old Indian page shows the numbers with no line, and a Moroccan mathematician added the line much later, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: In ancient India, a fraction was called bhinna, which means broken

final_answer.value: bhinna ('broken'); also bhaga or ansha ('part' or 'piece')

names.Leeza: mathematician (628 CE) who kept using the old Indian way of writing fractions

never_show: the your-turn answer: three fourths written the old way
maths_rules: the old Indian way writes the numerator above the denominator with no line, e.g. 1 above 2 for one half
the Bakshali manuscript, from around 300 CE, shows fractions written this way
Indian scholars from 499 CE to c. 850 CE, among them Leeza (628 CE), kept this way of writing for several centuries
a Moroccan mathematician of the 12th century introduced the line between numerator and denominator
the Indian way of writing reached Europe through the Arabs and came into general use there around the 17th century
names: bhinna means broken; bhaga or ansha means part or piece
slip: Keeko says the line was always there; it was added much later
video_script.design: One idea: the old name and the old way of writing fractions. The old page stays on the board from start to end. Wrong idea: the fraction line was always there.
